meta.title: LUZ: a light, usable and zero-dependency design system for the web
meta.description: LUZ (Light, Usable & Zero-dependency) is a design system of tokens, CSS and a little vanilla JavaScript that starts from what the browser already does: native HTML that comes styled, three color modes, one cascade layer you can always override, and no build step. Start a project with LUZ, or migrate it page by page.

light.nojs: With JavaScript on, the light of your hour is drawn here.
light.fact.1: Light takes only 1.3 seconds to travel from the Moon to Earth.
light.fact.2: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach us; if the Sun went out, it would take us that long to notice.
light.fact.3: In just one second, a beam of light could travel around the Earth 7.5 times along the equator.
light.fact.4: A ‘light-year’ does not measure time, but the distance light travels in one year, which equals nearly 9.5 trillion kilometers.
light.fact.5: Due to the time light takes to travel, when you look at the stars at night you are seeing them as they were tens, hundreds, or thousands of years ago.
light.fact.6: According to current physics, the speed of light in a vacuum is the cosmic speed limit; nothing with mass can travel faster than it.
light.fact.7: Light slows down to about 225,000 km/s when traveling through water due to the density of the medium.
light.fact.8: In a laboratory, scientists managed to slow light down to just 61 kilometers per hour by passing it through extremely cold sodium.
light.fact.9: A light (or radio) signal takes between 3 and 22 minutes to reach Mars, depending on how aligned the planets are.
light.alt.globe: A globe lit by the sun as it is now, its land a puzzle with one faint grey piece for each country: the day side faces the light, the night side fades.

hero.title: Design system for humans, ready for AI.
hero.lead: Tokens, CSS and a little vanilla JavaScript, built on what the browser already does: start a project with LUZ, or migrate it page by page. Every component works before JavaScript loads, and every change starts with a failing test.
why.title: Three words, one promise.
why.lead: A CSS-first, zero-build design system for the web. Your CSS always wins, JavaScript is only an enhancement, and every page works before it loads.
why.weight.caption: The gzipped weight each package publishes, measured in dist when this page is built.
why.usable.sub: Accessible by default, not by add-on.
why.usable.caption: Counted when this page is built; what is short of 100% is in the statement.
why.usable.access: Built to WCAG 2.2 AA and EN 301 549, the EU standard for accessible digital products. It starts from what the browser does well, adds visible focus, contrast and reduced motion, and checks them with axe on every change. Read the statement.
why.zero.sub: Your code, not a tree of someone else’s.
why.zero.caption: Counted in every package’s package.json when this page is built.
why.light.text: Plain CSS and small ES modules, from a CDN or from npm. No preprocessor, no compiler and no build step: what you read in the files is exactly what the browser runs, and each package has a size ceiling that never goes up.
why.zero.text: LUZ’s packages ship with no dependencies: only CSS and ES modules over what the browser already offers. Nothing to install to try it, no framework to keep up with, and nothing that breaks when another library ships a new major version.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.lead: Short answers to what people ask about LUZ: what it is, what it does to your HTML, how to use it and how to bring it into a site that already exists.
faq.what.a: LUZ is a design system for the web in three parts: tokens, core and the catalog, with prompts so an AI can build the site with you. It lets the browser do the work, checks instead of promising, and an AI can write it without making anything up.
faq.parts.q: What does each part of LUZ do?
faq.parts.a: Tokens hold the look, core styles your HTML and gives you components, and the catalog adds what a whole site needs. Tokens are the colors, scales, type and three color modes as CSS custom properties, and they work alone. Core is the reset, the style of every HTML element, the layout objects (o-container, o-stack, o-grid), the components (.luz-btn, .luz-card, .luz-tabs) and a little optional JavaScript. The catalog is pieces for the whole site, like search and the cookie banner.
faq.different.q: What makes LUZ different from the systems most people use?
faq.different.a: LUZ starts from the browser instead of from a framework: native HTML, no build step, any stack, and it works without JavaScript. Accessibility is checked, not promised: axe tests, every contrast computed in each mode, forced colors and reduced motion. It needs less markup, because HTML comes out complete without classes, and it is customized without a fight, with layers, :where() and tokens, never !important. It is ready for AI in a way you can verify: the prompts are generated from the packages, so they never carry an invented class.
faq.loses.a: LUZ falls short in community, in complex widgets (a date picker, a combobox, a data table), in components for React or Vue, and in maturity: it is still 0.x.
faq.classes.q: Do HTML elements have a style without any class?
faq.classes.a: Yes. With luz.css loaded, native HTML comes out complete without a class: text, lists, buttons, fields, forms and tables, with the space between blocks. Every rule sits inside :where(), so any rule of yours wins.
faq.unstyled.q: Which HTML elements have no style?
faq.unstyled.a: The tags that structure the page have no style, because the layout is yours: div, span, section, article, aside, header, footer, main, nav and form. body gets only the page's type and color. The tags the browser draws (option, em, q) and the invisible ones (meta, script, template) are left alone too.
faq.why-classes.q: What are the LUZ classes for, then?
faq.why-classes.a: The LUZ classes are for what HTML cannot say: a link that looks like a button (.luz-btn), a role with no HTML equivalent (danger, ghost, sizes), a component with markup of its own (a card, tabs, a field with its help and error) and the layout objects. What HTML can say is said in HTML: a button with no type is the primary one, aria-invalid marks an error, aria-current the active link and disabled what is off.
faq.same.q: Does an element look different with a class and without one?
faq.same.a: Very little. Without a class, an element looks as much as it can like its LUZ component; the class adds what needs markup or a role (grouping accordions, the parts of a modal, the bar of a code block). The class never undoes what the element gives.
faq.classless.a: Yes, LUZ is classless: native HTML comes out styled with no class. Unlike other classless systems, LUZ also has complete components with a class, a catalog for the whole site and three color modes.
faq.how.q: What is the best way to use LUZ?
faq.how.p0: The best way is six steps, with nothing to compile:
faq.how.ol1: Load luz-tokens.css, luz.css and luz.js from the CDN or npm.
faq.how.ol3: Add a class only for what HTML cannot say, and lay out with core's objects.
faq.how.ol4: Put your brand in with tokens: copy _template.css and change the values.
faq.how.ol5: From the catalog, link only what you use.
faq.how.ol6: JavaScript is optional: everything works without it.
faq.how.p1: The fast lane: paste the prompt for your kind of site into an AI and review the result with luz-check.
faq.js.q: Do I need JavaScript to use LUZ?
faq.js.a: No. Most LUZ components are CSS only, and the ones with a script work without it too. The page of each component says what you get without JavaScript.
faq.change.q: Can I change the default styles later?
faq.change.a: Yes, without fighting them. Tokens are the intended way to change the whole look, and your own CSS wins: LUZ is in cascade layers, so unlayered CSS beats it with no !important. What you do not override stays: change only the color of an h1 and it keeps LUZ's size.
faq.for.a: LUZ is for websites written in HTML, new or already built: a landing page, a blog, documentation, a company site. It fits any generator or CMS that produces HTML, Markdown included (Hugo, Astro, Eleventy), projects with no build step, and sites that must be accessible and work without JavaScript. An existing site can move to it piece by piece.
faq.not-for.a: LUZ is not for utility classes in the style of Tailwind, nor for React or Vue apps that expect their framework's components: LUZ gives HTML and classes. It gives no ready-made page structure (header, hero, footer) either: you write it, or the AI does.
faq.new-only.q: Is LUZ only for new projects?
faq.new-only.a: No. Start a project with LUZ, or migrate it page by page. A new project is where LUZ fits like a glove; one that already exists is migrated in islands with luz.conditional.css, which styles only what you mark, and the prompt guides each step.
faq.worth.q: Is it worth migrating a project that has its own design system?
faq.worth.a: For a multi-page or content site, yes, with a medium effort. For a single-page app on a React or Vue component library, no: you would change the look but end up rewriting the components anyway.
faq.migrate.q: How do I migrate a project built on another framework, and how does the AI help?
faq.migrate.p1: Migrate in phases, one page at a time, with one rule above all: the AI speeds up the mechanical work, and you decide and check. A migration breaks not from the new CSS but from deleting the old without knowing who used it.
faq.migrate.p2: Before touching anything, the AI takes the inventory (pages, framework components, the JavaScript that depends on classes, the !important), you take screenshots of each page, and a few smoke tests cover what must not break. Then the phases: tokens with your current brand; the old CSS in a layer before LUZ; a first small island by hand; page by page, one commit each; and only at the end, with nothing left using it, the old framework goes.
faq.migrate.p3: It hurts in three ways: two visual languages for a while, the duplicated weight while it lasts, and the old framework's JavaScript, which has to be rewritten. The AI never deletes anything without your OK.
fit.good.public: Content sites, documentation and public services that must meet WCAG 2.2 AA.
fit.good.server: Server-rendered pages and static sites, in any back-end language.
fit.good.own: Teams that want to read and own their CSS.
fit.bad.react: You need ready-made React or Vue components.
fit.bad.grid: You need a data grid, charts or a date-range picker: LUZ has none.
fit.bad.beta: You need a stable API today: LUZ is in beta, and names can still change.
